summary: This excerpt from the Wikipedia article on the 1973 oil crisis covers its effects on the car market and on Japan, and its trigger. The crisis cut demand for large American cars and boosted fuel-efficient Japanese imports, which led Japanese makers to build larger cars and later open US plants. It also describes Japan's heavy dependence on Arab oil and the October 1973 Yom Kippur attack that renewed pressure on oil prices, with the Shah of Iran defending higher prices.
one_line: The 1973 oil crisis boosted Japanese fuel-efficient cars, exposed Japan's dependence on Arab oil, and followed the Yom Kippur War and rising oil prices.
key_facts: Toyota and Nissan (then known as Datsun) introduced larger cars such as the Toyota Corona Mark II, Toyota Cressida, Mazda 616 and Datsun 810 after buyers lamented the small size of the first Japanese compacts.
The larger Japanese cars added air conditioning, power steering, AM-FM radios, power windows and central locking without increasing the price.

A decade after the 1973 oil crisis, Honda, Toyota and Nissan, affected by the 1981 voluntary export restraints, opened US assembly plants and established luxury divisions Acura, Lexus and Infiniti respectively.
The oil crisis reduced the demand for large cars.
Japanese imports such as the Toyota Corolla, Datsun B210, Honda Civic and Subaru DL had four cylinder engines that were more fuel efficient than typical American V8 and six cylinder engines.
The Mitsubishi Galant was a captive import from Chrysler sold as the Dodge Colt.
Unibody construction and front-wheel drive, used by Japanese imports, became de facto standards.
Japan was the country most dependent on Arab oil, with 71% of its imported oil coming from the Middle East in 1970.
On November 7, 1973, the Saudi and Kuwaiti governments declared Japan a "nonfriendly" country, and Japan received a 5% production cut in December, causing a panic.

On November 22, Japan issued a statement saying Israel should withdraw from all the 1967 territories and advocating Palestinian self-determination; by December 25 it was considered an Arab-friendly state.
On October 6, 1973, Syria and Egypt, with support from other Arab nations, launched a surprise attack on Israel on Yom Kippur.

Iran was then the world's second-largest oil exporter and a close US ally; the Shah of Iran said oil prices would rise, perhaps "ten times more", citing Western price increases of 300 percent on wheat, sugar and cement.
